claims.text: A defect-inclusive predictive framework will accurately capture the electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Explicit treatment of atomic-scale disorder, defects, and oxygen interstitials will reduce prediction errors by approximately 20–40% relative to perfect-crystal analytical models.
The relevant initial material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr prepared by arc melting and homogenization.
The comparison uses an oxygen-lean HfNbTaTiZr sample and a sample containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
A CPA-based or similar quantum effective-medium framework can explicitly model scattering contributions from defects and oxygen impurities in HfNbTaTiZr.
Testing in both oxygen-lean and oxygen-contaminated samples can isolate the effect of interstitial oxygen on electrical transport.
Oxygen interstitials in HfNbTaTiZr act as electron-scattering centers.
At low temperatures, impurity scattering from defects and oxygen raises the residual resistivity of HfNbTaTiZr.
At higher temperatures, the interplay between phonon scattering and defect-induced scattering alters the conductivity trend.
Representing defect and phonon scattering will produce a more realistic simulation of transport in non-ideal HfNbTaTiZr crystals.
The proposed framework will reproduce measured conductivity curves within approximately ±15% error.
Conventional perfect-crystal models will deviate from measured conductivity by more than approximately 30%.
The oxygen-contaminated HfNbTaTiZr specimen will have higher resistivity than the oxygen-lean specimen.
The model is applicable to bulk polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr containing up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model's accuracy for nanocrystalline HfNbTaTiZr or oxygen concentrations above 1 wt.% is untested.
The magnitude of the accuracy improvement may depend on defect distribution and microstructural details.
Residual resistivity ratios can be used to assess low-temperature defect scattering in these samples.
Activation energies derived from Arrhenius-type analysis are an appropriate high-temperature transport metric for HfNbTaTiZr.
A deviation above ±15% in either temperature regime or an error improvement below approximately 20% would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The claimed 20–40% error reduction is numerically inconsistent with a model error no greater than 15% and a conventional-model error greater than 30% if all values use the same relative-error metric; those bounds imply an error reduction greater than 50%.
